client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. There's this coffee shop she loved, and every time I walk past it or go inside, I just get hit with this wave of sadness that I can't seem to shake. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because it's not like anything can actually change what happened.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — grief like this is one of the most profound things we can carry, and that wave of sadness you feel near the coffee shop makes complete sense, because that place holds so much of her. You're right that nothing can change what happened, and I want you to know I'm not here to try to fix that or take the pain away. I'm curious though — when you imagine walking past that coffee shop, what's the very first thought that comes to your mind?

client: The first thought is usually something like, "She's never going to be in there again." It just hits me all at once, and then I feel this guilt because I keep thinking about how I didn't visit her as much as I should have in the last year. It's like the coffee shop and the guilt are all tangled up together now.
therapist: That thought — "she's never going to be in there again" — is such a painful reminder of a permanent loss, and it makes so much sense that grief and guilt have become intertwined in that space for you. I'd gently invite you to notice that the guilt you're carrying seems to come from a place of love — you *wanted* to be there more, which says something meaningful about how much she mattered to you. When you think back on the time you *did* spend with her, what do you imagine she would say about the kind of person you were to her?

client: I think she would probably say something kind, because that's just who she was. But honestly, it's hard for me to really take that in right now, because it almost feels like I'm just making up what I want to hear rather than facing the reality that I let her down. I guess I'm skeptical that thinking about what she might have said is going to actually change how guilty I feel.
therapist: That skepticism is really honest and worth honoring — you're not looking for a quick fix, and that makes a lot of sense given how real this pain is. What I'd gently offer is that the belief "I let her down" is worth examining not to make yourself feel better, but to make sure it's actually *accurate* — because guilt can sometimes tell us a story that feels true but isn't the whole picture. What actual evidence do you have, from specific moments or memories, that supports the idea you let her down — and is there any evidence that might complicate that story?

client: I mean, the evidence I have is that I kept telling myself I'd visit more and then I just... didn't. I got caught up in work and my own life, and there were probably three or four months where I barely saw her. But I guess if I'm being honest, there were also times I did show up, like when she was sick last winter and I took her to her appointments, so I don't know, it's not like I was completely absent.
therapist: It takes real courage and honesty to hold both of those things at once — the times you weren't there as much as you wanted, *and* the times you genuinely showed up when it mattered, like being by her side when she was sick. That's a much more complete and human picture than "I let her down," which leaves out so much of who you actually were to her. I'm wondering — if a close friend described their relationship with their grandmother in exactly the same way you just described yours, would you conclude that they had let her down?

client: No, I probably wouldn't say a friend had let their grandmother down if they described it that way — I'd tell them they were being too hard on themselves. But it feels different when it's me, like the standard I hold myself to is just way stricter, and I'm not sure why I can't seem to apply that same compassion to myself. I hear what you're saying, but knowing something logically and actually feeling it are two very different things.
therapist: You've just named something really profound — that gap between knowing something and *feeling* it is one of the most common and frustrating parts of grief and guilt, and it doesn't mean you're doing anything wrong. The fact that you hold yourself to a stricter standard is worth being curious about, because that pattern likely didn't start with your grandmother — it might be something that shows up in other parts of your life too. Where else do you notice yourself applying a harshness to yourself that you'd never direct at someone you care about?

client: Honestly, it shows up a lot — like at work, if I make a mistake I'll replay it for days, or with friends, if I cancel plans I convince myself they must resent me even when they say it's fine. I think I've just always been this way, so it feels less like a pattern I can change and more like just... who I am. I'm not sure I know how to be any different, even if I wanted to.
therapist: What you've just described — replaying mistakes at work, assuming friends resent you — sounds exhausting to carry, and I want you to know that recognizing it as a pattern is actually a really significant moment, because patterns are something that developed over time, which means they're not simply "who you are" in some fixed, unchangeable way. The fact that you can observe this tendency, almost like stepping outside yourself to notice it, suggests there's already a part of you that isn't fully defined by it. I'm curious — can you think of even one small moment, maybe recently, where you were able to treat yourself with even a little of the kindness you'd offer a friend?

client: I'm trying to think of a moment like that and it's actually really hard to come up with one, which is kind of uncomfortable to admit. Maybe the closest thing was last week when I was exhausted and I let myself leave work on time instead of staying late, and I didn't beat myself up about it too much. But honestly it feels like a pretty small and unremarkable thing to hold up as an example of self-compassion.
therapist: That moment is actually more meaningful than you're giving it credit for — you noticed what you needed, you acted on it, and you let yourself off the hook, which given everything you've shared about how hard you are on yourself, is genuinely not a small thing. I'd gently push back on the part of you that's already labeling it "unremarkable," because that same critical voice is doing the very thing we've been talking about — minimizing evidence that doesn't fit the story that you're somehow falling short. What do you think it would feel like to deliberately look for more moments like that one over the coming week, not to fix anything, but just to notice when that kinder part of you shows up?

client: I think it could be interesting to try, but I'm also a little worried that I'll spend the whole week looking for those moments and just not find any, which would probably make me feel worse. Or even if I do notice something, I might immediately second-guess whether it really counts, the same way I just did with the work example. I guess I'm open to it, but I don't want to set myself up for another thing to feel like I failed at.
therapist: That concern is so understandable, and honestly it shows real self-awareness that you can already anticipate how that critical voice might hijack the exercise — that's worth paying attention to rather than pushing through blindly. So let's make this as low-stakes as possible: instead of *looking* for moments, what if you just kept a tiny, informal note on your phone whenever something happens that you might normally dismiss, with zero pressure to evaluate whether it "counts"? What feels like the smallest, least overwhelming version of this that you could actually imagine trying without it becoming another thing to measure yourself against?

client: Maybe I could just send myself a quick text message when something happens, because that feels less formal than an actual note-taking app and I wouldn't feel like I was building some kind of record to be judged against. The thing I'm still a bit uncertain about is whether I'll even remember to do it in the moment, because usually when something small like that happens I'm just moving on to the next thing without stopping to notice. But I suppose if I forget most of the time and only do it once or twice, that's probably okay too.
therapist: You've just done something really important without perhaps realizing it — you anticipated a potential obstacle and then immediately offered yourself a compassionate "out," deciding in advance that once or twice is okay, which is exactly the kind of flexibility you've been struggling to give yourself. That instinct to be gentle with yourself about the experiment itself *is* the practice, in a way. I'm wondering — if you do manage to send yourself even one text this week, what do you think it might feel like to read it back?

client: I think reading it back might feel a little strange or even awkward, like catching myself being nice to myself in a way I'm not used to. There's a part of me that wonders if I'll just roll my eyes at it and think it sounds silly. But maybe there's also a small chance it might feel like a tiny bit of relief, like some proof that I'm not completely failing at everything, even in the middle of all this grief.
therapist: That glimpse of relief you just described — "proof that I'm not completely failing at everything" — feels really significant, especially because you found it yourself rather than me suggesting it, and it tells me that underneath all this grief and self-criticism there's a part of you that genuinely wants to be seen more fairly. The awkwardness you're anticipating makes complete sense too, because being kind to yourself is genuinely unfamiliar territory, and unfamiliar things often feel strange or even silly at first before they start to feel natural. I'm curious — what do you think your grandmother would feel if she could see you, right now, starting to question whether you deserve a little more of that kindness?
